lead: Burning fuel releases heat, and only about 30 percent of it reaches the crankshaft as useful work. The rest sits in the metal and must leave, or the piston rings lose their oil film and the liner scores. Cooling is the path that heat takes from the cylinder walls to the outside air. Two families do this job: air cooling, where fins on the outside hand heat straight to a moving air stream, and liquid cooling, where a coolant carries heat to a radiator. Motorcycles and small gensets use the first; cars and tractors, and larger gensets, use the second.
prereq: You need: engine components and the four-stroke cycle from Unit 1, and the meaning of brake power from Unit 5.

sections.h3: Why heat must leave the engine

blocks.text: Fuel energy does not all become work. In a typical diesel engine, of every 100 units of heat released by burning fuel, about 30 leave as brake power at the crankshaft, about 30 go out with the exhaust gas, about 30 pass into the coolant, and about 10 are lost to friction and radiation. The coolant share is a fixed tax the engine pays, and something must carry it away.

Metal sets the upper limit. Aluminium alloy pistons lose strength quickly a few hundred degrees above normal running temperature, so the crown must stay well below that. Lubricating oil sets a tighter limit: above roughly 150 °C the oil at the piston rings oxidises, turns to varnish and coke, and its film breaks. A broken film means metal touching metal, and the liner scores. The oil system that keeps this film alive is in 4.3.

Uneven cooling is as harmful as no cooling. If one side of the head runs hot and the other cold, the two sides expand by different amounts, thermal stress builds up, and the head can warp or blow its gasket. Too much cooling also hurts: a cold engine vaporises petrol badly, wears faster and gives lower efficiency. The aim is a target metal temperature, not the coldest possible engine.

blocks.where: Q is the heat carried away per second in kW; ṁ is the coolant mass flow in kg/s; c is the specific heat of the coolant in kJ/kg·K (4.18 for water); ΔT is the temperature rise of the coolant in K.

sections.h3: Air cooling: fins, baffles and a blower

blocks.text: An air-cooled engine carries no coolant. Thin metal fins are cast or machined on the barrel and head. Each fin adds surface, so the same metal wall can hand its heat to a much larger area of air. Heat passes from the hot metal into the air that flows between the fins, and the moving air carries it away.

Fin spacing is a compromise. Fins packed close together give more area on paper, but the air trapped between them becomes stagnant and stops removing heat. Spacing is chosen so that fresh air keeps touching metal along the whole gap. Fin thickness is kept small to save weight and space, but thick enough that heat can still conduct out to the tip; the real bottleneck is the air side, which removes heat far more slowly than the metal conducts it.

The air must be made to flow. On a motorcycle road speed does the job. A stationary genset or pump set has no road speed, so a blower or fan pushes air and sheet-metal baffles guide it between the fins instead of letting it slip around the outside of the engine. Baffles also stop the same air from being reused.

Air cooling suits motorcycles, scooters, small gensets, pump sets and aircraft piston engines. It has no radiator, no pump and no coolant to freeze or leak, and it warms up fast. Its weakness is that air carries little heat per kilogram, so the metal runs hotter, the head runs hotter than the barrel, and power per litre is limited.

sections.h3: Liquid cooling: jacket, radiator, pump, thermostat

blocks.text: A liquid-cooled engine wraps the hot parts in a jacket: a hollow space cast into the block and head, running close to the liner, the valve seats and the exhaust port. Coolant in the jacket picks up heat, a pump pushes it to the radiator, and air flowing over thin tubes and fins takes the heat out of it. Some syllabi call this indirect cooling, because the air never touches the hot metal.

The circuit has four parts. The water pump is a small centrifugal pump driven by a belt or gears. The radiator is the heat exchanger. The fan pulls air through the radiator when the vehicle is slow or standing. The thermostat is a valve filled with wax: it stays shut while the engine is cold, so the engine warms up quickly, then opens at its set temperature and lets coolant through the radiator.

Liquid removes far more heat from a given area of metal than air does, so the jacket stays compact and all cylinders run at nearly the same temperature. The price is weight, cost, pump power and parts that can leak. Circulation by pump, by density difference, and under a pressure cap that raises the boiling point is covered in 4.2.

examples.question: A genset engine burns 8 kg of diesel per hour. The calorific value of the diesel is 42 000 kJ/kg. Thirty percent of the fuel energy leaves through the coolant. The cooling water is allowed to rise 6 K. Take the specific heat of water as 4.18 kJ/kg·K. Find (a) the fuel power, (b) the heat rate carried by the coolant, (c) the coolant mass flow in kg/s and in kg/min.
steps: Convert the fuel flow to kg/s: ṁf = 8 kg/h ÷ 3600 s/h = 2.222 × 10⁻³ kg/s.
Fuel power is fuel flow times calorific value: Pf = 2.222 × 10⁻³ kg/s × 42 000 kJ/kg = 93.33 kW. This is the fuel power, not the nameplate rating.
The coolant takes 30 percent of the fuel power: Q = 0.30 × 93.33 kW = 28.0 kW.
Rearrange Q = ṁ c ΔT for the flow: ṁ = Q ÷ (c ΔT) = 28.0 kW ÷ (4.18 kJ/kg·K × 6 K) = 28.0 ÷ 25.08 = 1.12 kg/s.
Convert to per minute: 1.12 kg/s × 60 s/min = 67 kg/min.
examples.answer: Fuel power is 93.3 kW, the coolant carries 28 kW, and the required coolant flow is about 1.12 kg/s, that is 67 kg per minute.
examples.check:
fuel_kg_h = 8
cv = 42000
fuel_power = fuel_kg_h * cv / 3600
q = 0.30 * fuel_power
c = 4.18
dT = 6
m_dot = q / (c * dT)
print(round(fuel_power, 2))
print(round(q, 2))
print(round(m_dot, 2))
print(round(m_dot * 60, 1))

traps: Starting the coolant calculation from the brake power on the nameplate. The coolant takes a share of the fuel energy, so start from fuel flow times calorific value.
Calling the thermostat a temperature sensor. It is a wax-filled valve that opens and closes the coolant path; the fan and the gauge are separate.
Saying an air-cooled engine has no cooling medium. Air is the medium; the heat still leaves by convection, only through fins instead of a jacket.
Mixing units in Q = ṁ c ΔT. With c in kJ/kg·K the answer is in kW; using c = 4180 J/kg·K with kJ elsewhere gives a factor of 1000 error.
Saying the radiator cools the engine. The radiator cools the coolant; the jacket is what touches the hot metal.

quiz.q: Name the two families of engine cooling systems and give one application of each.
quiz.a: Air cooling (motorcycles, small gensets) and liquid cooling (cars, tractors). Some syllabi call the liquid type indirect cooling.

quiz.q: What is the job of the thermostat in a liquid cooling system?
quiz.a: It is a wax-filled valve that stays shut while the engine is cold so warm-up is quick, and opens at a set temperature to send coolant through the radiator.

quiz.q: Why are cooling fins spaced apart instead of being packed tightly together?
quiz.a: Air trapped in very narrow gaps becomes stagnant and stops carrying heat away. Spacing is chosen so fresh air keeps touching metal along the whole gap.

quiz.q: Why is overcooling harmful to an engine?
quiz.a: A cold engine vaporises fuel poorly, has higher friction and efficiency loss, and corrosive condensation forms in the oil. The goal is a target metal temperature, not the coldest possible engine.

quiz.q: A petrol engine burns 5 kg of fuel per hour with a calorific value of 44 000 kJ/kg. Twenty-eight percent of the fuel energy goes to the coolant. Find the fuel power and the heat rate to the coolant.
quiz.a: Fuel power = 5 × 44 000 ÷ 3600 = 61.11 kW. Coolant heat rate = 0.28 × 61.11 = 17.11 kW.

quiz.q: A genset installed in a small closed room runs hotter than the same genset kept outdoors. Explain using the air-cooling mechanism.
quiz.a: Air cooling depends on a steady supply of cool air and on the temperature difference between metal and air. In a closed room the room air heats up, the temperature difference falls, and the fins remove less heat per second, so metal temperature rises until heat out equals heat in.

quiz.q: Why does an air-cooled engine usually make less power per litre than a liquid-cooled engine of the same size?
quiz.a: Air removes less heat from a given surface, so the head and barrel run hotter and can approach the oil breakdown limit. Mixture strength and compression ratio must then be kept conservative to avoid knock and ring coking, which caps power per litre.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern engine thermal management treats cooling as a controlled system, not a fixed circuit: electric pumps and electronically controlled thermostats hold metal temperature at a chosen value instead of letting it float. Exhaust gas recirculation coolers and charge-air intercoolers borrow the same jacket-and-radiator logic, and oil coolers now often share the engine coolant loop. Battery packs and traction motors in electric vehicles use liquid cold plates designed exactly like a block jacket. Search terms worth following: engine thermal management, split cooling, coolant control valve, cold plate.
